title: Learning as optimisation: loss, gradients, autodiff
summary: Training a model means minimising a loss by walking downhill along its gradient. Learning rate, momentum and local minima decide whether training succeeds; automatic differentiation computes the gradients.
outcomes: define a loss function and explain why we minimise it
carry out gradient descent steps by hand
explain the effect of the learning rate and momentum
say what automatic differentiation does and why SciML depends on it
narration_en: How does a network learn? We define a loss: a single number that measures how wrong the model is, such as the average squared difference between predictions and data. Learning means finding the weights that make the loss small. Imagine the loss as a landscape of hills and valleys over all possible weights. Gradient descent stands on this landscape, feels which way is downhill, and takes a step. The gradient tells the direction, and the learning rate sets the step size. Too small and training crawls. Too large and it jumps across valleys or even flies off. Real landscapes have many valleys, called local minima, and momentum, which keeps some of the previous step, can help roll past small ones. Popular optimisers such as Adam adapt the step for each weight. Computing gradients by hand is impossible for millions of weights, so software uses automatic differentiation, which applies the chain rule exactly. SciML uses the same machinery to differentiate a network with respect to its inputs, which is how physics enters the loss.
narration_ar: كيف تتعلم الشبكة؟ نعرّف دالة خسارة: رقماً واحداً يقيس مقدار خطأ النموذج، مثل متوسط مربع الفرق بين التنبؤات والبيانات. والتعلم يعني إيجاد الأوزان التي تجعل الخسارة صغيرة. تخيل الخسارة تضاريس من تلال ووديان فوق كل الأوزان الممكنة. يقف الانحدار التدرجي على هذه التضاريس، ويتحسس اتجاه النزول، ثم يخطو خطوة. يحدد التدرج الاتجاه، ويحدد معدل التعلم طول الخطوة. إذا كان صغيراً جداً زحف التدريب، وإذا كان كبيراً جداً قفز فوق الوديان أو طار بعيداً. وفي التضاريس الحقيقية وديان كثيرة تسمى القيم الصغرى المحلية، ويساعد الزخم، الذي يحتفظ بجزء من الخطوة السابقة، على تجاوز الصغيرة منها. وتكيّف خوارزميات شائعة مثل Adam طول الخطوة لكل وزن. وحساب التدرجات يدوياً مستحيل لملايين الأوزان، لذا تستخدم البرمجيات الاشتقاق التلقائي الذي يطبق قاعدة السلسلة بدقة. ويستخدم تعلم الآلة العلمي الأداة نفسها لاشتقاق الشبكة بالنسبة إلى مدخلاتها، وهكذا تدخل الفيزياء في دالة الخسارة.

diagram.title: The training loop
diagram.caption: Predict, measure the loss, compute gradients by automatic differentiation, update the weights, repeat.

nodes.label: Predict
nodes.detail: Run the model on training inputs to get predictions.

nodes.label: Loss
nodes.detail: For example mean squared error, (1/N) Σ (prediction − data)². Physics terms can be added (module 1.5).

nodes.label: Gradient
nodes.detail: The vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to every weight.

nodes.label: Automatic differentiation
nodes.detail: Software (PyTorch, JAX) records each operation and applies the chain rule backwards to get exact gradients.

nodes.label: Update
nodes.detail: Take a step downhill. η is the learning rate. Momentum and Adam modify this step.

nodes.label: Weights
nodes.detail: The adjustable parameters. After many updates they settle in a valley of the loss.

tour.text: Make predictions and measure how wrong they are with the loss.
Automatic differentiation computes the gradient: which way is downhill.
Step downhill by the learning rate times the gradient.
Updated weights give new predictions, and the loop repeats.

sections.heading: Loss functions
sections.html:
A loss turns 'how wrong' into one number. The most common is the mean squared error:

L(w) = (1/N) Σ (ŷᵢ(w) − yᵢ)²

Squaring makes all errors positive and punishes big ones more. In SciML we add terms that measure how badly the model breaks a physical law; minimising the total balances data and physics.

sections.heading: Gradient descent by hand
sections.html:
Take L(w) = (w − 3)², gradient 2(w − 3), start w = 0, learning rate η = 0.1:

w₁ = 0 − 0.1 × 2 × (0 − 3) = 0.6; w₂ = 0.6 − 0.1 × 2 × (0.6 − 3) = 1.08

Each step closes 20% of the gap to the minimum at w = 3. With η = 1.0 the step overshoots to w = 6, then back to 0: it never settles. With η above 1.0 it diverges.

sections.heading: Momentum, Adam and local minima
sections.html: Real losses are bumpy, with many valleys. Momentum keeps a fraction of the last step, like a ball rolling, so it can pass small bumps and move faster along gentle slopes. Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015) adapts the step size for each weight and is the default for training physics-informed networks. Stochastic gradient descent uses random mini-batches of data, which adds helpful noise.

sections.heading: Automatic differentiation
sections.html: Automatic differentiation (autodiff) records every arithmetic operation in the model and applies the chain rule backwards (backpropagation). It gives exact derivatives, not finite-difference approximations, at a cost similar to one extra model evaluation. Crucially for SciML, autodiff can also give the derivative of the network's output with respect to its input, such as dŷ/dt, which is exactly what a differential equation needs.

callouts.title: Try it
callouts.html: In the explorer, find a learning rate that reaches the deep valley near w = 4.3 without momentum. Then set momentum to 0.9 with a small learning rate.

callouts.title: How SciML uses it
callouts.html: In a physics-informed network, autodiff gives dŷ/dt at any time t; the loss then penalises dŷ/dt + k ŷ ≠ 0. You will build exactly this in module 1.5 and Go 2.

code.title: Gradient descent and a numerical gradient check
code.source:
import numpy as np
L  = lambda w: (w - 3)**2
dL = lambda w: 2*(w - 3)
for lr in [0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 1.1]:
    w = 0.0
    for _ in range(20):
        w -= lr * dL(w)
    print(f'learning rate {lr}: w after 20 steps = {w:.3f}')
h = 1e-5
print(f'gradient at w=1: exact {dL(1.0)}, finite difference {(L(1+h) - L(1-h))/(2*h):.4f}')
code.explain: Small rates converge, 1.0 oscillates forever, above 1.0 diverges. Autodiff gives the exact gradient that finite differences only approximate.
code.expected:
learning rate 0.1: w after 20 steps = 2.965
learning rate 0.5: w after 20 steps = 3.000
learning rate 1.0: w after 20 steps = 0.000
learning rate 1.1: w after 20 steps = -112.013
gradient at w=1: exact -4.0, finite difference -4.0000

takeaways: A loss turns 'how wrong' into one number; training minimises it.
Gradient descent steps downhill: w ← w − η × gradient.
The learning rate must be neither too small nor too large; momentum and Adam help.
Automatic differentiation computes exact gradients, including with respect to inputs.
